text: Thousands of cars burning gasoline, in a tube under a river. How does the Holland Tunnel breathe?
Opened in 1927, it runs over a mile and a half under the Hudson, New Jersey to Manhattan.
The killer was carbon monoxide. Tests at Yale and the Bureau of Mines found just four parts in ten thousand was dangerous.
Chief engineer Clifford Holland died in 1924, before it opened. Ole Singstad designed the ventilation, and finished it.
His answer: split the tube into three layers.
Fans blow fresh air into a duct under the roadway. It rises through slots along the curb.
Dirty air is pulled up through vents in the ceiling, into an exhaust duct above, and out.
Four ventilation buildings, two on land and two out in the river, hold eighty-four fans. Forty-two blow in. Forty-two pull out.
Together, they can replace all the air in the tunnel every ninety seconds.
It was the world's first mechanically ventilated tunnel. Today it's a National Historic Landmark.
What should we take apart next?
Congrats! You've discovered how the Holland Tunnel breathes.
